analysis.one_liner: Creates a public Medicare-based health plan anyone could buy and expands ACA subsidies.
analysis.headline: The public-option bill never left committee, ending with the 118th Congress without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Choose Medicare Act would have let almost anyone buy a public health plan run by Medicare (called "Part E"), offered through the ACA exchanges and as a voluntary option for employers, with gold-level benefits including abortion and reproductive coverage regardless of state bans. It would also have made ACA premium subsidies richer and permanent, capped out-of-pocket costs in traditional Medicare at $6,700 a year, and put $30 billion into a fund to lower premiums and copays. It was referred to three House committees and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying coverage on their own would get a new public plan option with gold-level benefits, including abortion coverage that state bans could not block. ACA enrollees at every income level would get bigger subsidies, and for the first time households above 400% of the poverty line would qualify permanently. Workers at jobs with unaffordable or skimpy insurance could be referred to enrollment help, and the public plan would follow them if they lost their job. People on traditional Medicare would get a hard annual out-of-pocket cap starting at $6,700 in 2026, which traditional Medicare has never had. Insured patients would gain from limits on balance billing by the plan's providers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: ACA enrollees, the uninsured, and Medicare beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Creates Medicare Part E public plans sold in the individual, small-group, and large-group markets through the exchanges, each a gold-level qualified health plan covering all essential health benefits plus everything Medicare covers, including abortions and all reproductive services that state laws could not prohibit.

Opens eligibility to any U.S. resident not already on Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP, lets any employer voluntarily offer the plan, requires the government to act as third-party administrator for employer plans on request, and guarantees people can keep the plan if they lose their job.

Every provider participating in regular Medicare on enactment day automatically joins the public plan, payment rates are negotiated to land between Medicare rates and the average commercial exchange rate, and Medicare's balance-billing limits apply.
Extends Medicare's prescription drug negotiation program, and the related excise tax penalty on manufacturers that refuse to negotiate, to drugs covered by the public plan.
Caps annual out-of-pocket cost-sharing in traditional Medicare at $6,700 starting in 2026 (adjusted for medical inflation), protection traditional Medicare beneficiaries do not have today.

Rebases ACA premium subsidies on the second-cheapest gold plan instead of a silver plan, permanently removes the 400% of poverty income cap on subsidy eligibility, and expands cost-sharing reductions so lower-income enrollees' plans cover up to 94% of costs.

Appropriates $2 billion in startup funding plus initial claim reserves, and $30 billion for 2025-2027 for state reinsurance payments or direct help with copays, coinsurance, premiums, and deductibles.

Extends the large-group market's use of employer-size-based premium variation rules and strengthens federal and state rate review so excessive or discriminatory rates can be denied, modified, or rebated, including for grandfathered plans.
Requires employers that do not offer affordable, minimum-value coverage to refer full-time workers to an exchange navigator for enrollment help, and funds navigator capacity.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund $2 billion in startup costs, open-ended reserves, the $30 billion reinsurance and affordability fund, and the permanently expanded premium subsidies. Private health insurers would face a public competitor for their individual, small-group, and large-group customers. Hospitals and doctors would be paid more than Medicare but less than typical commercial rates in the public plan, and could not balance-bill participating-plan patients beyond Medicare limits. Brand-name drug makers would face Medicare-style price negotiation on a new pool of patients.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, private insurers, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: The public plan is not free coverage: its premiums must fully finance both benefits and administrative costs, so its affordability depends entirely on the rates it negotiates, and a plan that attracts sicker enrollees could struggle to stay cheaper than private options.
The $30 billion reinsurance fund can be paid directly to private insurance issuers to cover high-cost enrollees, which cushions insurers' losses rather than only helping patients directly.
Removing the 400% of poverty cap on subsidy eligibility is permanent and open-ended federal spending with no stated price tag, on top of the roughly $32 billion in explicit appropriations.

Payment rates capped below average commercial rates could push some hospitals and doctors to limit how many public-plan patients they take, despite the bill's requirement to maintain network adequacy, and the automatic participation rule for Medicare providers relies on current law that Congress could later change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and concrete: a genuine public alternative to private plans, bigger and permanent ACA subsidies, a first-ever out-of-pocket cap in traditional Medicare, and drug-price negotiation applied to the new plan. The costs are real but modest relative to federal health spending: about $32 billion in explicit appropriations plus an open-ended subsidy expansion, and the $30 billion fund partially routes money to private insurers rather than exclusively to patients. The main design risk is that a premium-financed public plan competing against insurers could face adverse selection and rate pressure from providers. On balance, the bill's benefits to ordinary people outweigh its costs, which fall mostly on taxpayers generally, private insurers, hospitals, and drug makers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees and then a health subcommittee until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, never getting a markup, a hearing, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Jimmy Gomez introduced the Choose Medicare Act on May 1, 2024, joined by Representatives Don Beyer, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Jared Huffman as original cosponsors.
The bill's total support in the House was four members, all Democrats; no Republican cosponsored it.

The Speaker referred it to three committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means — a routing that requires the bill to clear multiple committees before it can reach the floor.

On May 3, 2024, it was referred to a Health subcommittee, and it was referred to a Health subcommittee again on December 17, 2024; in its entire seven-month life the bill received no markup, no hearing, and no vote.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, brand-name drug makers, and hospital systems that would have faced a public competitor and Medicare-style rates are better off because the bill died; the existing ACA market structure, where subsidies flow through private plans, remains in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and drug makers kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split appears only in sponsorship, where it was 4 Democrats to 0 Republicans.

industries.note: The bill creates a direct public competitor for their individual, small-group, and large-group customers, with government-set rates between Medicare and commercial levels. But it also hands them a $30 billion reinsurance fund and permanently richer subsidies that flow through their exchange plans, cushioning the blow.

Every Medicare-participating provider is automatically in the public plan, bringing a new pool of insured patients, but payment rates are capped between Medicare and average commercial rates and balance billing is restricted.

The bill applies Medicare's drug price negotiation program and its excise tax penalty for refusing to negotiate to drugs covered by the public plan, exposing a new pool of prescriptions to negotiated prices.
